slides.0.title: Montagne de Reims
slides.0.subtitle: The hill of Pinot Noir and nine Grand Cru villages
slides.1.title: Location and landscape
slides.1.highlights.0.title: A half-moon around Reims
slides.1.highlights.0.content: The area forms a half-moon around Reims, roughly 20 miles east to west and 3 to 6 miles wide, a broad headland carpeted with woodland and thickets between the Vesle and Marne rivers (Comité Champagne)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Pinot Noir country
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Pinot Noir is the most common grape here, and its body and structure form the backbone of many NVs and Blanc de Noirs
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Varied aspects
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Slopes face south, east and north, and aspect with soil decides which grape does best, so the same hill also carries Chardonnay and Meunier
slides.1.highlights.3.title: The region with most Grand Crus
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Nine of the 17 Grand Cru villages are here, the most of the four sub-regions
slides.1.content: Remember this hill: Pinot Noir plus nine Grand Crus.
slides.2.title: The nine Grand Cru villages
slides.2.highlights.0.title: INAO list
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Ambonnay, Beaumont-sur-Vesle, Bouzy, Louvois, Mailly-Champagne, Puisieulx, Sillery, Verzenay and Verzy
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Bouzy and Ambonnay
slides.2.highlights.1.content: On south-facing slopes, known for rich, red-fruited, full-bodied Pinot Noir (common description, not a rule)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Verzenay and Mailly-Champagne
slides.2.highlights.2.content: On the northern to north-eastern side of the hill, known for tighter, structured, higher-acid Pinot Noir (common description, not a rule)
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Check: variety limits
slides.2.highlights.3.content: The INAO specification sets no variety limit for these nine villages; the tendencies come from terroir and custom, not from the text of the rules
slides.2.content: All nine are in the Marne département; the Aube has no Grand Cru at all.
slides.3.title: Premier Cru and surroundings: pockets of Chardonnay and Meunier
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Examples from the specification list
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Premier Cru examples around the Montagne: Ludes, Chigny-lès-Roses, Rilly-la-Montagne, Villers-Allerand, Montbré, Taissy and Cormontreuil (full list in the INAO specification)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Islands of white grapes
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Villers-Marmery and Trépail (Premier Cru) on the eastern side are known for Chardonnay, the white-grape pocket of the Montagne (common description)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: The western Petite Montagne
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Villedommange, Sacy and Écueil (Premier Cru) in the west, often called the Petite Montagne, carry more Meunier (common description)
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Villages outside the list
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Only listed villages may use Grand or Premier Cru; for any other village the name must be preceded by Vigne de or Vignoble de (specification)
slides.3.content: One hill, three characters: a Pinot Noir core, Chardonnay pockets and a Meunier west wing.
slides.4.title: Style role and still wines
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Role in the blend
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Pinot Noir supplies frame, body and red fruit, forms the core of many NVs and is a main source of Blanc de Noirs
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Coteaux Champenois
slides.4.highlights.1.content: The AOC covers still white, rosé and red wines with at least 9% natural alcohol, over the same area as Champagne
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Bouzy rouge
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Still red wine from Bouzy (and others such as Ambonnay) is well known, but the specification covers Coteaux Champenois as a whole and has no separate article for Bouzy
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Naming a village
slides.4.highlights.3.content: When a village or cadastral lieu-dit is named, all base-wine grapes must come from it and the name may not be printed larger than the AOC name
slides.4.content: Next we go south: the Marne Valley and the Côte des Blancs.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
How many Grand Cru villages are in the Montagne de Reims?
Montagne de Reims 9, Vallée de la Marne 2 and Côte des Blancs 6 make 17 in total.
Which of these is a Grand Cru village of the Montagne de Reims?
Verzenay is in the Montagne de Reims; Avize, Cramant and Oiry are in the Côte des Blancs.
Which wines does the Coteaux Champenois AOC cover?
A. Still white, rosé and red wines
INAO specification: Coteaux Champenois covers still white, rosé and red wines.
